sentence: These readings depend on aspect and context, rather than a rule that quise always means "tried" or no quise always means "refused." Learners who\'ve already sorted out the [broader preterite-versus-imperfect split](/preterite-vs-imperfect/) still trip on this group specifically, because the meaning shift is larger than "completed vs. ongoing." It\'s closer to two different English verbs mapping onto the same Spanish root.
note: Current aspect target supports only the referenced broader completed-whole versus ongoing viewpoint; quise/no quise qualification is on the source and is not attributed to that target. Ser/estar target supports two words corresponding to English to be; no fixed automatic meaning shift asserted.
target_quote: coreSummary: 'The preterite (canté) presents a past action as a completed whole, with a clear edge. The imperfect (cantaba) presents a past action or state in progress, without marking where it started or ended. How long something took doesn\'t decide the choice: a preterite action can span years and an imperfect one can span seconds. What decides it is the angle the speaker takes on the action.',

sentence: One more contrast worth having next to this one: [ser and estar](/ser-vs-estar/) split English "to be" the way saber/conocer splits "to know," and the underlying move for both pairs is the same: stop translating the English word, and ask what kind of claim the sentence is actually making.
note: Current aspect target supports only the referenced broader completed-whole versus ongoing viewpoint; quise/no quise qualification is on the source and is not attributed to that target. Ser/estar target supports two words corresponding to English to be; no fixed automatic meaning shift asserted.
target_quote: coreSummary: 'Ser identifies and defines: identity, origin, inherent characteristics, time, and material. Estar locates and describes a state: location, condition, and the result of a change. The common shorthand "ser is permanent, estar is temporary" breaks down often enough (someone can be permanently dead and use estar, or be only briefly a student and use ser) that it\'s more reliable to ask whether the sentence is defining the subject or reporting its current condition.',
